headline: VaultRelink uses local AI to recover lost notes from Markdown archives
summary: This open-source tool scans wiki links in your notes, identifies broken targets, and suggests replacements using a multilingual MiniLM model.
details: VaultRelink is a new open-source tool designed to help users recover lost connections within their local Markdown archives. It scans for wiki links, identifies targets that no longer exist, and then proposes potential replacements based on semantic similarity and lexical overlap.

The tool utilizes the sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 model, running entirely locally after an initial download. This ensures user privacy and allows for inspection of the code, with the option to replace the model in future versions.

VaultRelink generates a local HTML report that displays suggested replacements alongside excerpts from actual notes. This allows users to review the evidence before making any changes to their archive, preserving the original link's display text.

The core AI model was tested on a synthetic dataset, achieving high accuracy in retrieving intended notes. While this benchmark doesn't guarantee performance on real-world vaults, it demonstrates the model's potential.

The scanner supports a subset of Obsidian link resolution, but does not yet implement alias support or heading validation. Query context may be truncated, and the ranking system is fallible, meaning generated reports could contain sensitive note excerpts. A fictional demo vault is included for safe exploration.

headline: Apple's new MacBook Pro supports new color modes for pros
summary: The latest MacBook Pro features an OLED display and touchscreen, but its standout feature for color professionals is support for Apple CMF 2026 color modes.
details: The new MacBook Pro boasts an OLED display and touchscreen, but its most significant advancement for color professionals is its support for Apple CMF 2026 color modes. This technology aims to ensure that images appear consistent across different display technologies and for various viewers, addressing limitations of the older CIE 1931 standard.

CMFs, or color-matching functions, mathematically represent human color perception. While CIE 1931 has been the standard for decades, newer display technologies like OLED and quantum dots reveal its shortcomings, as biological variations in human eyes can lead to perceived color differences. Apple CMF 2026 is designed to overcome these issues.

This isn't the first time Apple has implemented this technology; it was previously featured on the Studio Display XDR. However, bringing it to a portable laptop significantly benefits professionals who need accurate color representation on the go.

The MacBook Pro offers two Apple CMF 2026 reference modes: one for P3 color primaries and another that includes both P3 and Adobe RGB primaries. It also supports a peak brightness of 2,000 nits for both HDR and SDR content, with True Tone automatically adjusting settings based on ambient light.

Beyond the new CMF standard, the MacBook Pro includes 14 additional reference color modes using the CIE 1931 color space, catering to various professional needs, including DICOM for medical imaging. It also features Apple Pro Display Calibrator for custom adjustments.

Apple's work on the Apple CMF 2026 standard, in collaboration with a CIE technical committee, is a crucial step towards ensuring current display technologies render colors identically for a wider audience. This advancement is particularly important as display technology continues to evolve rapidly.

The inclusion of Apple CMF 2026 on the MacBook Pro, priced at $2,900, makes this advanced color technology more accessible to a broader range of professionals compared to the more expensive Studio Display XDR. This move empowers mobile professionals with enhanced color accuracy tools.
